title: CLAY COUNTY BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Clay County Board met Tuesday evening at the courthouse in Louisville and worked quickly through their agenda.

In Chairman Joe Goodman’s absence, Vice Chair Barb McGrew called the meeting to order.  After the roll was called with Goodman, Terry Hronec and Rod Franklin absent, McGrew asked and then received board approval of the meeting agenda.  With no visitors seeking to address the board, Members went on to approve the Claims Committee Report.  Janice Brooks reported Paid Claims totaled $5.539.881 with Unpaid Claims of $179,807.

Next, Kasey Kemme County with the U of I Extension Office for Clay, Effingham, Fayette and Jasper Counties spoke to the board about its summer activities.   Kemme also introduced new Clay County Coordinator Breanna Shull of Dieterich, who was unable to attend Tuesday’s meeting due to a prior commitment.  In addition to Shull, she said there are three other full-time employees for Clay County, Megan Pierson, Michelle Hoffman and Erin Maxwell.  Kemme went on to describe many of the activities local 4-H Youth are involved in,  She stated there are 228 members of local 4-H clubs with 1,000 4-H Projects.  Club members are preparing to display at the upcoming Clay County Fair starting July 24.

The board was presented with the FY2025 Audit from Kemper CPA in Olney.  Members approved acceptance of the report, that did not mention any findings.  The report is available for public inspection in the Clay County Clerk’s Office in the courthouse.

Clay County Coroner Bryce Henry presented his semi-annual report for the period ending May 31.  Henry explained how the funding for his office works and stated that he is seeking the purchase of a vehicle following the appropriate guidelines and will return as the process moves forward.  In his report, which the board accepted, Henry states there were 71 total deaths, 70 of which were from natural causes and one was considered accidental from a motor vehicle crash.  The coroner’s office oversaw the performance of three autopsies.  A total of 31 cremation permits were issued.  There were three body donations, two coroner notifications and one pending case.  The coroner’s office conducted 23 investigations.  There were 11 hospital related deaths, 28 nursing/assisted/CILA cases, 29 residential deaths and three listed as other.

In the absence of Clay County Supervisor of Assessments Kindal Eastin. Vice-Chair Barb McGrew presented two reappointments to the Board of Review, Bad Rudolphi and Jack Hastings both to two-year terms.  She also sought to reappoint Dennis Holdenbrink to the Farmland Assessment Review Committee for a three-year term.  The board unanimously approved all three.

Clay County Hospital CEO/President Bob Sellers presented the hospital report.  He stated construction is underway for the expansion of the hospital for the Clay County Health Department.  Sub-contractors are being sought for the construction of the maintenance building with the hope of beginning construction in July with completion before snow flies.  Sellers also informed the board that the 340B program is completed for another year for acquiring medications at discounted prices.  He further stated that all CCH Physicians are locked into contracts for the next five years.  In action items, the board approved Sellers request for medical staff credentials and then voted unanimously to approve the purchase of a handheld ultrasound device at a cost of $54,464, to replace the ten-year-old version used now by Dr. Kumar.  Due to changes in technology, images are not transferable to patient records, meaning they cannot bill for it.  That will change with the addition of the new device.

Clay County Health Department Administrator Jeff Workman presented the Board of Health Report.  The board was asked to approve the Health Department’s FY2027 budget.  After a brief discussion, the board approve the health department’s $5,271,446 budget,  He reported that the State of Illinois has approved its FY2027 Budget that included many increases, however the local health protection grant was not included.  The Southern Illinois Public Health Consortium had written to the state in support of adding $10 Million to the previously funded $20 Million, however the request has apparently fallen on deaf ears.  Workman said the next S.U.R.E. Symposium is set for July 11 at Oil Belt Christian Service Camp.  He also briefly touched on other issues including the outbreak of Ebola cases in Africa and worries it could spread to other countries.  There was a concern recently that someone presented to a hospital ER in Chicago with possible symptoms for Ebola.  However, it turns out the person was experiencing two other diseases that are treatable.  Workman emphasized that no Ebola cases have been identified in the United States.  He did say though that measle cases continue to grow and its important that vulnerable people are given the measles vaccination.  Before taking a seat Workman asked the board to reappoint three members to the Board of Health for three year terms ending June 30, 2029.  The board approved the reappointment of Dr. Brandon Cycholl, Joe McCoy and Larry Rinehart.  Workman also invited Cancer Survivors to participate in the Bridge Study, that addresses cancer related stress during treatment.  Participants are paid for their information.  Call the Clay County Health Department to learn more.  At (618) 662-4406

Clay County Sheriff Andy Myers presented his report and stated they are seeking bids to replace the roof of the Clay County Courthouse.  The current roof dates to the 1990’s.  The sheriff also spoke about the need to discuss options for the next budget and to include the purchase of body cams.   Myers also spoke about an agreement reached between Clay City Schools and his office for them to help fund a School Resource Officer (SRO).  He stated the sheriff’s office will need to hire one additional deputy in the coming months as a result of the agreement.  The board agreed to the proposal.  Sheriff Myers then asked to revisit the issue of how Cannabis Tax Funds are distributed.  Currently, the money is divided evenly between the Sheriff’s Office and the D.A.R.E. program.  He says it would be more efficient to change the split from 50/50 to 75/25.  The board agreed to his request, effective July 1st.  Myers final action item was making a donation of a no longer used squad vehicle to the Clay City Fire Protection District, which members quickly did.

Vice Chair Barb McGrew presented bridge aid petitions for board consideration in the absence of highway engineer Darin Koelm.  All were approved and are evenly funded with 50 percent from Clay County and the other half from the specific Townships.  The first is a culvert project on Blair Township Lane and Acts Rd. with a cost of $15,000.  Next a culvert project in Xenia Township on Honey Locust Lane and Boxwood Rd. at a cost of $10,000.  The third and final project with a cost of $15,000 in Larkinsburg Township on Mockingbird Rd. for drainage improvements.

In Executive Finance, Barb McGrew called on Clay County District Attorney Phillip Givens to speak about the hiring of an Assistant District Attorney.  Givens explained that he had a vacancy and Cole Hildebrand is returning to Clay County after serving a stint in Jasper County.  Givens stated that he seeks to increase the salary for the position by partially using a small portion of Opioid stipend funds as they are intended to be used.  That puts the salary for that position above $100,000.  Hildebrand returns to the position next week.

During the Chairman’s Report, Vice Chair Barb McGrew presented a number of action items that had to do with CEFS and its Rural Bus Service.  The operation was formerly operated out of Shelby County and is now handled by Effingham County.  The board voted to rescind its Transportation Ordinance.  They also voted to rescind the Intergovernmental agreement with Shelby County.  Next, the board approved the Transportation Ordinance with Effingham County and then voted to approve a new Intergovernmental Agreement with Effingham County.  Leaders want to stress that nothing changes about rural bus service.  Everything remains the same as before.

title: QUILT SHOW
full_story:
The Sew Nifty Sisterhood Quilt Guild is having the “Oh My Stars” America 250th birthday celebration Quilt Show, raffle, and silent auction.

The show will be at the North Clay Elementary School, south building, on Friday June 19th from 5 to 7 pm and Saturday, June 20th from 9:00 to 4:00 pm.  Admission to the show is $5.00 per person and those 12 and younger get in for free.  There will be a raffle for a “Our flag stands for freedom” quilt with tickets on sale at the door or from any guild member.  There will also be a scavenger hunt and a silent auction.

Cathy Billingsley and Trudy Hurd from the Sew Nifty Sisterhood will be the guests today at 2 pm on the ReVue talking about the quilt show.

For more information go to the Sew Nifty Sisterhood Quilt Guild on Facebook.

title: CLAY COUNTY SHERIFF’S ACTIVITY REPORT
full_story:
Clay County Sheriff Andy Myers presented his monthly activity report during Tuesday’s Clay County Board meeting.  In the Report for May, the Sheriff’s Office issued a total of 26 Traffic Citations, made 34 Criminal Arrests and served 22 various Civil Papers.  A total of 19,999 miles were driven by Sheriff’s personnel during the month.

27 people were processed through the Clay County Jail during May.  There were 5 inmates in jail at the beginning of the month and 5 in jail at the end of the month.  The average daily jail population was 5.

Also, the Clay County Sheriff’s Office received a total of $3,032 during the month.  This includes:

The Sheriff’s Office handled approximately 528 complaints, 103 of which originated in Louisville and 88 in Clay City.  The Sheriff’s Office conducted 32 Criminal Investigations and 12 Accident Investigations during May.

title: CCH SPORTS PHYSICALS
full_story:

title: SUMMER FOOD SERVICE PROGRAM
full_story:
The Clay County Health Department’s Beyond the Bell program is participating in the Summer Food Service Program this summer.  Free meals, which meet Summer Food Service Program federal guidelines, are available to all children 18 years of age and under and to persons over 18 years of age who are enrolled in a state approved educational program for the mentally or physically disabled.  The Food Distribution Program is available to all eligible participants without regard to race, color, national origin, age, sex, or handicap.  Any person who believes that he or she has been discriminated against in any USDA-related activity should write immediately to the Secretary of Agriculture, Washington, DC 20250, or call toll free (866) 632-9992 (Voice).  Individuals who are hearing impaired or have speech disabilities may contact USDA through the Federal Relay Service at (800) 877-8339 or (800) 845-6136 (Spanish).  USDA is an equal opportunity provider and employer.

Free meals will be provided at the Beyond the Bell program from through August 13th.

Breakfast will be served at Beyond the Bell to program participants from 8:00 to 9:00 am and lunch will be served from 11:30 am to 12:00 pm.  Menus for both meals will be posted on Beyond the Bell’s Facebook page.

Clay County Health Department, the program sponsor, is located at 601 E. 12th Street in Flora.  For further information, contact Tamara Byers or Kathryn Holstlaw at 618-662-8322.

title: IECC CHANCELLOR
full_story:
The Illinois Eastern Community Colleges Board of Trustees is expected to affirm the appointment of Dr. Timothy L. Taylor as the next Chancellor of Illinois Eastern Community Colleges at its June 16th meeting at Olney Central College.  Dr. Taylor, who currently serves as President of Shawnee Community College, would assume the chancellorship on August 15th, pending Board approval.

The selection follows several months of transition planning by the Board of Trustees to ensure a smooth leadership transition following Chancellor Ryan Gower’s retirement on June 30th.

Dr. Taylor brings more than two decades of community college leadership experience to the position, including service as President of Shawnee Community College and previous leadership roles within Illinois Eastern Community Colleges.  Throughout his career, he has been recognized for his commitment to student success, workforce development, institutional effectiveness, strategic planning, and the mission of rural community colleges.

Board Chair Gary Carter said Dr. Taylor’s experience, leadership style, and understanding of the region made him the clear choice to lead the institution into its next chapter.

“Tim understands our communities, our mission, and the important role community colleges play in creating opportunity,” said Carter.  “Over the past several years, Illinois Eastern Community Colleges has undertaken significant work to strengthen and position the institution for the future.  The Board believes Tim has the experience, judgment, and leadership skills necessary to build upon that foundation and continue advancing IECC as one institution serving students and communities across all four campuses.”

During his tenure at Shawnee Community College, Dr. Taylor led initiatives focused on strengthening institutional effectiveness, improving financial stability, enhancing strategic planning and accountability systems, expanding partnerships with schools and employers, securing investments in facilities and infrastructure, and increasing opportunities for students throughout the region.

Taylor said he is honored by the opportunity to serve Illinois Eastern Community Colleges and excited about the future of the institution.

“I am honored by the confidence the Board of Trustees has placed in me,” said Taylor.  “Illinois Eastern Community Colleges has a proud history of serving students and communities throughout southeastern Illinois.  The institution is well-positioned for the future, and I look forward to working alongside the Board, employees, students, and community partners to build upon the strong foundation already in place.  Together, we will continue expanding educational opportunities, strengthening our communities, and ensuring IECC remains responsive to the changing needs of the region we serve.”

Board Chair Gary Carter also expressed appreciation for Dr. Gower’s decade of leadership at IECC and more than thirty-one years of service to higher education.

“Ryan’s tenure as Chancellor has transformed IECC,” Carter said.  “He led the institution through the COVID-19 pandemic, a successful accreditation reaffirmation, the implementation of Guided Pathways, the creation of the Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning, and the construction of seven new facilities across the district.  He championed investment in our campuses, our employees, and our students.  Most importantly, he led Illinois Eastern’s transformation from a multi-college system into a single college operating across four campuses under a unified leadership structure and shared vision.  His leadership has positioned IECC well for the future.  The Board and I are grateful for Ryan’s service and wish him and Tracey every happiness in retirement.”

Illinois Eastern Community Colleges serves southeastern Illinois through Frontier Community College in Fairfield, Lincoln Trail College in Robinson, Olney Central College in Olney, and Wabash Valley College in Mount Carmel.

title: COUNTERFEIT BILLS
full_story:
Local and area law enforcement authorities are alerting the public after reports of counterfeit $100 bills circulating in the area.

According to law enforcement the fake bills may appear legitimate at first glance but are marked “For Motion Picture Use,” indicating they are not legal tender.

Customers and businesses are urged to carefully inspect $100 bills before accepting them and to watch specifically for the printed phrase “For Motion Picture Use.”

Anyone who encounters suspicious currency should report it immediately and exercise extra caution during cash transactions.

title: LAWS TAKING EFFECT JULY 1ST
full_story:
While Illinois families won’t see gas prices increase July 1st, they will see a record $55.9 billion budget with over $800 million in tax increases and new laws take effect.

Referred to as Deb’s Law, patients with a terminal disease may ask a doctor to prescribe aid-in-dying medication allowing them to end their life “in a peaceful manner.”  Senate Bill 1950 was originally titled “Sanitary Food Preparation” and amended in the last week of the 2025 regular session to the “End-of-Life Options for Terminally Ill Patients Act.”

House Bill 3851 adds to the bullying prevention section of the school code.  “Posting or distributing sexually explicit images” is considered a form of bullying.  Beginning in the 2026-2027 school year, “‘cyber-bullying’ also includes the posting or distribution of an unauthorized digital replica by electronic means” if the post creates fear or harm for the student, hurts the student’s physical or mental health, or interferes with the student’s academic performance or the ability to participate in other services, activities or privileges provided by the school.

A school bus driver has a new permit option.  House Bill 2962 creates a specialized school bus driver permit to operate smaller passenger vehicles and a “multifunction school activity bus” designed to carry up to 15 passengers when being used for curriculum-related activities such as transportation between home and school, to a vocational school or for a field trip.  The bill gives districts more flexibility for curriculum-related transportation while maintaining strict safety standards.

House Bill 1226 raises the age for in-person license renewal to 79, up from 75.  The bill also adds to the Illinois Vehicle Code that an applicant over age 87, or 75 if the person holds a commercial driver’s license, “must prove, by actual demonstration,” that they can safely operate a vehicle.

Passed in 2024 during the 103rd Illinois General Assembly, Senate Bill 1 streamlines bureaucracy and accomplishes a recommendation from the bipartisan Illinois Commission on Equitable Early Childhood Education and Care Funding.  Two years after Pritzker signed it into law, the new Department of Early Childhood launches July 1st, overseeing programs and services that have been handled by three state agencies.

title: TICK SPECIES SPREADING
full_story:
Social media is abuzz with news about ticks and tick-borne diseases actively spreading across Illinois, with many counties confirming several species.

Some of the increased talk comes from more awareness of ticks and their dangers, Jenny Buttaccio, Illinois Lyme Association (ILA) communications director, told FarmWeek.

However, Illinois has ticks converging from the north and south.  Different tick species at different life stages are peaking at different times.  “So, it is very alarming,” said Samantha Kerr, the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH)’s vector surveillance and control program manager.

Many Illinois counties have lone star ticks, blacklegged ticks and dog ticks.  Several counties have all three, according to the IDPH tick surveillance maps.

“The geographic range of different species is expanding,” said Chris Stone, University of Illinois medical entomologist, who noted the Gulf Coast tick is also present in southern and parts of central Illinois.

The blacklegged tick, associated with Lyme disease, was more concentrated in northern Illinois, but is trickling south to central Illinois.  At the same time, the lone star tick that can cause Alpha-gal syndrome, an allergic reaction to red meat, is moving from the south toward central Illinois.  Illinois is already in the top 13 states of Alpha-gal cases in the nation, Buttaccio said.

Part of the uptick of ticks in Illinois is due to warmer winters and longer, warmer seasons.  The invasive Asian longhorned tick, which attacks large livestock rather than people, is also a threat in Illinois.  Information about ticks and their diseases in Illinois is available on the Illinois Tickborne Disease Dashboard website experience.arcgis.com.

Last month, US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. announced major initiatives to strengthen the nation’s response to Lyme disease and other tick-borne illnesses, including a multi-million-dollar pilot program focused on tick control and funding for researchers to combat Alpha-gal syndrome.

Kerr said the general advice of avoiding tick habitats is harder for farmers to follow when they are mowing grass, repairing fences and doing other outdoor work.  She recommends the use of Environmental Protection Agency-registered insect repellents, wearing permethrin-treated clothing, using a lint roller to remove possible ticks, doing a thorough tick check and showering within a couple of hours of potential exposure.

You can have a big impact on protecting yourself by doing small things, Stone said.  Wear long pants and clothing treated with permethrin, “It’s cheap and easy to do.”
